```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(AKCatchments)
options(AKCatchments.cache = file.path(tempdir(), "ak_vignette_cache"))
```

Catchment means of the PRISM 30-arc-second (~800 m) monthly and annual
normals for Alaska, 1981-2010 (PRISM Climate Group and NPS Alaska
Inventory and Monitoring, 2018): mean, minimum and maximum temperature
and precipitation. These are the normals behind the NPS basin descriptors'
monthly climate columns.

Input, as for every layer: catchments (sf polygons with `site_code`, one
row per catchment, any CRS; a single `ak_delineate()` result, a list of
them, `ak_catchments()` output or your own polygons). Chunks that download
data are not run when this vignette is built; chunks that only compute
are. The other layers are listed in `vignette("delineation")`, section 7.

## 1. Getting the data

Automatic, once per variable and period (an ARC ASCII grid in a zip) into
the cache's `prism_ak_8110/` folder. The grids run across the date line
(longitude 172-237 E), which the package handles. `ak_prefetch()`
downloads all 52.

## 2. Using it

```{r use, eval = FALSE}
d <- ak_delineate(lat = 63.7255, lon = -148.9670, site_code = "SITE-001")   # one catchment
ak_climate_normals(d)                                        # one catchment (PRISM 1981-2010 by default)

x <- ak_catchments(pts)                                  # many: data frame of site_code, lat, lon
x <- ak_climate_normals(x)                                   # columns appended to x, provenance recorded
ak_provenance(x)

ak_climate_normals(sf::read_sf("hand_catchments.gpkg"))   # your own polygons with site_code
```

Only some grids: `ak_climate_normals(x, vars = c("tmean", "ppt"), periods = c("07", "annual"))`.
Normals from Daymet over 1991-2020 instead (matching the anomalies of
`weather_at_samples()`): `ak_climate_normals(x, "daymet4", weather = w)`,
with `w` from `ak_weather()`; see `vignette("weather-daymet")`.

## 3. What you get

`prism_<var>_<period>` (°C or mm; periods `01`-`12` and `annual`) and
`prism_flag` (`tmean_not_mid`, `annual_mismatch`, `out_of_order`).

## 4. Uncertainty: how it is computed

No error is published for these grids. `prism_flag` marks internal
inconsistencies (monthly mean not between min and max, annual not
matching the months), the way bad values show up. An alternative is the
difference between PRISM and another normals product (TerraClimate,
CHELSA, or Daymet's own 1991-2020 climatology) as an empirical spread.

## 5. Checking and validating it

Compare with Daymet's own climatology over 1991-2020 (a different period,
method and station set): a spread between the two products is an
empirical uncertainty where PRISM gives none.

```{r compare, eval = FALSE}
w <- ak_weather(x, years = 1991:2020)
x |>
  ak_climate_normals(vars = "tmean", periods = "07") |>                       # PRISM 1981-2010
  ak_climate_normals("daymet4", vars = "tmean", periods = "07", weather = w) |> # Daymet 1991-2020
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::transmute(site_code, prism_tmean_07, daymet_tmean_07, diff = daymet_tmean_07 - prism_tmean_07)
```

Expect Daymet's 1991-2020 to be warmer by the warming between periods;
site-to-site differences beyond that are product disagreement.

## 6. Pitfalls

- 1981-2010, not 1991-2020: don't mix with Daymet baselines without saying
  so.
- 800 m cells against small catchments: one or two cells.
- Terms: free with attribution; confirm redistribution of derived tables.

## References

- PRISM Climate Group, Oregon State University, and NPS Alaska Region Inventory and Monitoring (2018). 1981-2010 climate normals for Alaska, 30 arc-seconds.
